title: Predicting numbers
blurb: Not every answer is a category — sometimes AI predicts a number. Meet the line of best fit.

steps.title: Two kinds of questions
steps.body:
So far your AIs answered **which kind?** — cat or dog, rose or daisy. That's called **classification**.

But some questions don't have categories. *"How tall will this plant grow?"* *"What will this house sell for?"* The answer is a **number**. Predicting a number has its own name: **regression**.

steps.title: Which is which?
steps.question: "How many points will the team score tonight?" — what kind of problem is this?
steps.explain: It's regression — the answer is a number (a score), not a category.

steps.title: The big idea: draw a line
steps.body:
Here's the trick. If you have a bunch of examples — say, *hours studied* vs *test score* — you can draw a **straight line** through them.

Then, to predict a new score, you just read the line. The whole challenge is: **which line is the best one?**

steps.title: Your turn — find the best line
steps.body:
Below are some data points. Press **Fit the line** and the computer draws the single best straight line through them.

The orange dashes show each **miss** — how far off the line is from each dot. Then try dragging the dots and watch the line chase them.

steps.title: Fit the line
steps.body: Press Fit the line, then drag the red dots around and watch the line and the error change.

steps.title: What is that 'error' number?
steps.body:
Every orange dash is a **mistake** — the gap between a real dot and the line's guess. Add up all those gaps (squared) and you get the **error**, also called the **loss**.

**The best line is the one with the smallest error.** That's literally how the computer chooses it: try lines, keep the one that misses the least.

steps.title: Reading the error
steps.question: One line has an error of 2 and another has an error of 40. Which line fits the points better?
steps.explain: Smaller error = closer to the dots = better fit. Error 2 wins.

steps.title: This is how AI 'learns' — for real
steps.body:
Pause on this, because it's huge: **learning = lowering the error.**

Whether it's this little line or a giant AI with billions of settings, training is the same loop: make a guess, measure how wrong it is, adjust to be a little less wrong, repeat. You just watched it happen.

steps.title: The learning loop
steps.question: In one sentence, what does 'training' an AI really mean?
choices: Making the error as small as possible
steps.explain: Exactly — training means adjusting the model until the error is as small as it can be.

steps.title: When a straight line isn't enough
steps.body:
Real life isn't always a straight line. Sometimes the pattern curves.

You *could* draw a wild, wiggly line that hits **every** dot perfectly… but that's usually a trap. Here's why.

steps.title: The overfitting trap
steps.body:
A line that bends to touch every single dot has basically **memorized** the examples instead of **learning** the pattern.

Give it a new dot it hasn't seen and it flails. This is called **overfitting** — being so obsessed with the practice questions that you bomb the real test. A simpler line that's 'close enough' usually predicts new data better.

steps.title: Spot the overfit
steps.question: An AI scores 100% on its practice data but terribly on new data. What probably happened?
choices: It overfit — it memorized instead of learning the pattern
steps.explain: Classic overfitting: it memorized the practice set and never learned the general pattern, so new data trips it up.

steps.title: Why predicting numbers matters
steps.body:
Regression is everywhere grown-ups use AI:

- 🏠 estimating house prices
- 🌡️ forecasting tomorrow's temperature
- 📈 predicting how many people will show up

All the same idea you just did: fit a line (or curve) to past examples, then read off a prediction.

steps.title: Recap
steps.question: What's the goal when fitting a line to data?
choices: Get the smallest total error without overfitting
Make the line as steep as possible
steps.explain: Smallest error, but not by memorizing — a simple line that generalizes beats a wiggly one that overfits.

steps.title: What you learned 🎉
steps.body:
- **Classification** predicts a category; **regression** predicts a **number**
- The **line of best fit** is the one with the smallest **error (loss)**
- **Training = lowering the error**, step by step — the heart of all AI
- **Overfitting** = memorizing instead of learning; simpler often generalizes better

**Next up:** a different kind of AI you can actually *read* — the **decision tree**.
